title: O2 – Historical perspectives: Fayol, Weber, Follett, Taylor
source: Zusammenfassung von Session 2 „Historical Perspectives – Work“ (Olivier Wurtz)

blocks.text: Organisation and management theory developed in four periods (Richard Scott), along two axes: closed vs open system and rational vs social individual.

Large organisations appeared with industrialisation (Chicago slaughterhouses, Coca-Cola). Three changes created the modern company: new industries, labour law (work contracts, subordination) and directors (control passes from owners to managers; business schools).
The founding figures – Fayol, Weber and Taylor – favour a rational, universal and scientific approach (“one best way”). Mary Parker Follett adds the human and social side.
Organise to produce efficiently – “order through formal rules”: Weber, Taylor, Fayol (directive management).
Motivate – “group, morale and work conditions”: Mayo, McGregor, Maslow, Herzberg (human relations).
Adjust the structure – “the organisation is shaped by outside forces”: Chandler, Lawrence & Lorsch, Woodward, Perrow (contingency and planning).
Motivate through culture – “complexity, change, turbulence and adhocracy”: Weick, March, Ouchi, Simon, Crozier, DiMaggio & Powell (participative management, culture and leadership).

19th century: very small, family companies; workers were craftspeople, the owner supervised directly. Companies then grow (rural exodus) and need skilful leaders and managers between owner and workers. Strong trust in science (positivism).
What turned small family firms into modern companies:
children: Emergence of new industries and sectors
Labour law: work contracts create a subordination link
Appearance of “directors”: control passes from owners to managers; creation of business schools

blocks.text: Adam Smith (1776) first formalised the economic value of the division of labour (the pin factory).

sections.heading: Henri Fayol (1841–1925) · the manager and the hierarchy

blocks.text: French mining engineer and top manager; “Administration industrielle et générale” (1916) – one of the first management books.
Technical · commercial · financial · security · accounting · administrative. The administrative function – planning, organising, leading, controlling – was ignored before Fayol.

Rationality and efficiency: division of labour, order, discipline · Top-down authority: centralisation, scalar chain, unity of command, unity of direction, authority · People: stability of tenure, initiative, esprit de corps · Rewarding: remuneration, equity · Subordination of individual interest to the general interest.
Physical, mental, moral, education, technical, experience.
Mining context (gas, floods, landslides): unity of command and the quality of supervisors were vital.
German sociologist: instead of asking why people break rules, he asked why they obey.
Traditional (custom, “it has always been so”) · charismatic (devotion to an exceptional leader) · rational-legal (stable, explicit, impersonal rules; people obey the function, not the person).

Aims at precision, speed, clarity, regularity, reliability, efficiency. Principles: rational rules; authority exercised by impersonal function; legal demarcation of roles; selection on technical qualifications, appointment, fixed salary; life-long careers; strict discipline and operating rules.
Red tape, slowness, lack of creativity, complex rules. Merton: goal displacement – the rules become more important than the objectives behind them.

sections.heading: Mary Parker Follett (1868–1933) · the human side

blocks.text: “Mother of modern management”, forerunner of the human relations movement.

Integrative conflict resolution (integrate perspectives instead of domination or compromise) · “power with” instead of “power over” · groups, not individuals, are the primary unit of organisational life.
Engineer at Midvale Steel; “The Principles of Scientific Management” (1911).
A powerless hierarchy: workers practise “soldiering” (working below capacity to avoid ever-rising targets) and control the know-how, so they choose their own methods.
Three building blocks:
children: Observe 10–15 skilled workers, divide work into tasks, time each task, remove useless gestures → the one best way
Selection (“the right man in the right place”) and individual performance pay (+30 % to +100 %)
Supervision separated from production: four functional foremen per worker and a powerful methods department

blocks.text: Result: vertical division (design vs execution) and horizontal division (specialised tasks). Taylorism survives today (call centres, fast food, logistics).
